result.summary: CivicCore v1.2.0 is a Python library of shared, storage-neutral primitives (auth, audit, ingest, LLM, platform contracts, connector sync, security, search, notifications, onboarding, scheduling, release provenance, testing). It ships no HTTP server, no end-user app, and no enforcement layer — it provides ABCs, dataclasses, Pydantic schemas, SQLAlchemy ORM, decorator registries, and an Alembic migration runner that consumer modules opt into. Modules ride on civiccore by importing helpers and inheriting the shared SQLAlchemy `Base`; nothing forces them to. CivicAccess v0.4.0 pins `civiccore==1.2.0` for a release-wheel hash and for the package to be loadable by the desktop's bundled python-services health check, but in its own runtime code it touches civiccore only to read `__version__` for `/health` — it reimplements its own DB writer guard, schema-migrations table, and audit_events table instead of using `civiccore.auth`, `civiccore.migrations.runner`, or `civiccore.audit`. That gap (declared dependency vs. actual consumption) is the headline finding.

contracts_modules_must_satisfy: Declare civiccore as a pinned dependency in pyproject.toml. Convention is the published release-wheel URL with SHA-256 (CivicAccess: `civiccore @ https://github.com/CivicSuite/civiccore/releases/download/v1.2.0/civiccore-1.2.0-py3-none-any.whl#sha256=...`). City-core modules pin v1.2.0 exactly; the desktop module_registry blocks city-core entries that don't match (see civiczone blocked at 1.1.0).

If using LLM, prompt templates, model registry, ingestion, audit, task queue, or shared schema — inherit civiccore primitives, do NOT reimplement. Stay off the reserved placeholder packages `civiccore.catalog` (ADR-0001), `civiccore.exemptions` (ADR-0002), `civiccore.scaffold` (ADR-0003) until they ship in a versioned release.

Migration ordering: when a module runs Alembic, its env.py must call `civiccore.migrations.runner.upgrade_to_head` BEFORE its own migrations so the baseline (`alembic_version_civiccore`) is installed first. Module migrations live under their own version_table to avoid collision. (The desktop's civicsuite_runtime.migrate enforces this order: civiccore first, then per-module.)

ORM models that share tables with civiccore must inherit `civiccore.db.Base` so they share one DeclarativeBase metadata registry (per the v1.2.0 ingest pipeline contract on `documents`/`document_chunks`/`data_sources`).

Module manifest (when wired into the desktop) must conform to `civiccore.platform.ModuleManifest`: module_id matches `^[a-z][a-z0-9-]{1,63}$`, declares `civiccore_min_version`, services typed via `ServiceType` literal, no `docker|wsl|linux_shell|terminal` runtime requirements for the windows_local profile, route permissions cross-reference declared permission keys, services reference declared health_check ids, no self-dependency. `validate_windows_local_manifest` raises on violation.

Auth (when adopting shared contract): use `civiccore.auth.authorize_bearer_roles` with a `<MODULE>_AUTH_TOKEN_ROLES` env var holding JSON `{token: [roles]}`; or `civiccore.auth.staff_key_gate(env_var, header)` for the `X-Civic*-Role: staff` + `X-Civic*-Staff-Key` convention; or `civiccore.auth.authorize_trusted_header_roles` + `enforce_trusted_proxy_source` for reverse-proxy SSO with `<MODULE>_TRUSTED_PROXY_CIDRS`. Suite-session bearer requires `CIVICCORE_SUITE_SESSION_SECRET` (≥16 chars, placeholder-free) and may share revocation via `CIVICCORE_SUITE_SESSION_REVOCATION_FILE`.

Audit (when adopting shared chain): use `AuditHashChain` for new events or `compute_persisted_audit_hash`/`verify_persisted_audit_chain` for the legacy CivicRecords-AI pipe-delimited row format. Events MUST set `source_module` for cross-module audits.

Task handlers (when joining the shared queue): register via `@civiccore.tasks.register_task_handler(task_type)` at import time; the worker reads `CIVICCORE_TASK_HANDLER_MODULES` (comma-sep) to import them; requires `DATABASE_URL` pointing at the shared Postgres holding `civiccore_local_tasks`.

Connector sync (when implementing a live connector): use `SyncCircuitState`/`SyncRetryPolicy`/`apply_sync_run_result` for retry+circuit semantics and `build_sync_operator_status`/`build_sync_source_status` to expose health to operators; do not reinvent the 5-failure/2-in-grace breaker.
Search access tiers: use `access_level_allows`/`filter_records_by_access_level` with a module-owned rank map (civiclegal demonstrates the pattern) rather than hand-rolling privilege checks.

LLM template resolution: callers register with `consumer_app=<module>` so override resolution traverses DB → in-memory OVERRIDE_REGISTRY → civiccore default in that order; the consumer FastAPI app mounts `model_registry_router` and injects its DB session.

Backup/restore: declare `ModuleBackupHook` entries naming relative-path globs (CivicAccess: `Data/workflows/access`, `Data/exports/access`, `Data/files/access`) and assemble manifests with `build_backup_manifest` so the shared restore plan stays checksum-verified.

Security/config: validate secrets at startup via `validate_secret_setting`/`validate_fernet_key_setting`/`validate_password_setting`/`looks_like_placeholder`; encrypt secret-bearing config at rest with `encrypt_json`/`decrypt_json`; reject blocked hosts with `validate_url_host`/`validate_odbc_connection_string`.

Release provenance (when cutting a release): pin per-repo+per-tag workflow identity, publish `release-attestation.json` + Sigstore bundle, run `verify_release_provenance` before promoting. Org-wide wildcards are rejected.

Reserved placeholders: ADR-0001/0002/0003 forbid any module from importing or claiming dependency on `civiccore.catalog`, `civiccore.exemptions`, or `civiccore.scaffold`; local equivalents must be ADR-documented as a temporary bridge.
result.what_civicaccess_inherits: CivicAccess's pyproject.toml pins civiccore==1.2.0 by release-wheel URL + SHA-256 (`civicaccess @ ... civiccore-1.2.0-py3-none-any.whl#sha256=a94ce958...`). What that pin actually buys CivicAccess in its current code (v0.4.0): (1) ONE symbol — `from civiccore import __version__ as CIVICCORE_VERSION` in civicaccess/main.py:7, used to report civiccore version in `/health`. That is the ONLY runtime civiccore import in civicaccess source. (2) The verify.yml CI gate asserts `civiccore.__version__ == '1.2.0'` so a wrong pin breaks CI. (3) Module loadability under the desktop's bundled python-services (civicsuite_runtime.services calls `importlib.import_module('civicaccess.main')`, which would fail if its `from civiccore import __version__` couldn't resolve). (4) Eligibility for the city-core profile — the desktop module_registry blocks city-core entries whose `civiccore_requirement` isn't 1.2.0 (civiczone is blocked at 1.1.0 for this reason). What CivicAccess does NOT inherit despite the pin: it does NOT use `civiccore.auth` (rolls its own constant-time `hmac.compare_digest` against `CIVICACCESS_TRUSTED_WRITE_TOKEN` and the `X-CivicAccess-Write-Token` header in main.py instead of `staff_key_gate` or `authorize_bearer_roles`), does NOT use `civiccore.migrations.runner` (uses an ad-hoc `civicaccess.schema_migrations` table and `metadata.create_all` in access_review.py:111 — schema is `civicaccess-windows-local-state-v1`), does NOT use `civiccore.audit` (writes a plain `civicaccess.audit_events` table with event_id/action/subject_id/actor/created_at and NO `previous_hash`/`current_hash` linkage — there is no hash chain at all on accessibility records), does NOT use `civiccore.tasks` (no task handlers registered, the `accessibility-review`/`records-export` tasks listed in modules.json are not wired to the civiccore queue worker), does NOT use `civiccore.platform.ModuleManifest` (the manifest fields in installer/modules.json are author-time JSON, not produced from the Pydantic model — the runtime never validates against `validate_windows_local_manifest`), does NOT use `civiccore.search`, `civiccore.llm`, or `civiccore.ingest`. The pin is therefore mostly a release-line marker plus version-string source — the substantive contracts civiccore offers are available but unused. The desktop supervisor compensates for the auth gap by injecting `CIVICACCESS_TRUSTED_WRITE_TOKEN` (supervisor.rs:386-2047) and the supervisor's shared `DATABASE_URL` is opportunistically picked up by `_review_database_url` for Postgres with SQLite fallback.
notable_gaps: Placeholder packages by design: `civiccore.catalog` (ADR-0001), `civiccore.exemptions` (ADR-0002, the 50-state public-records exemption engine), and `civiccore.scaffold` (ADR-0003, module generator CLI) are reserved namespaces with explicit no-consumption rules. README markets the exemption engine as platform scope; the package is a single docstring.
`civiccore.ingest` ships the pipeline but no scheduler/runtime — modules must own queueing and ingestion orchestration (CivicRecords AI keeps Celery + Beat for this).
`civiccore.onboarding` ships storage-neutral interview helpers but no web UI or persistence router.
`civiccore.search` is normalization + RRF + access filtering helpers; no search engine, no indexer, no vector retrieval (modules pair these with pgvector queries themselves).
`civiccore.notifications` ships deadline planning and compliance checks but no delivery queues, no SMTP/SMS adapter, no outbound orchestration.
`civiccore.scheduling` ships cron validation + next-run math but no scheduler runtime (no equivalent of Celery Beat).
`civiccore.verification` ships browser-evidence helpers; sovereignty verification is explicitly future work.

No HTTP server in civiccore. The LLM `model_registry_router` is just an `APIRouter`; consumers mount it and provide the session dependency override. There is no central `/admin/models` until a host app mounts the router.
No first-party identity provider. OIDC browser-session handling lives in module repos (CivicClerk's `oidc_auth.py` is marked as a future extraction candidate per ADR-0009 in that repo).

No enforcement that consumers actually use civiccore primitives. ModuleManifest validation runs only when `build_module_registry` or `validate_windows_local_manifest` is called — installer/modules.json entries today are hand-authored JSON and the desktop does not appear to validate them against the Pydantic model at boot. Several modules (CivicAccess, CivicNotice, Civic311, CivicBoards) ship parallel ad-hoc `X-CivicXxx-Write-Token` HMAC guards instead of `staff_key_gate`; CivicAccess ships its own `schema_migrations` table and a plain `audit_events` table without hash chaining. CivicCore offers contracts but does not police compliance.
Vendor write-back, credential orchestration, and vendor-specific network adapters are explicitly unshipped (README §Status). Modules that need them roll their own (CivicClerk's vendor-live-sync).

Task queue requires PostgreSQL (`civiccore_local_tasks` uses JSONB and `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`); there is no SQLite fallback for the queue itself even though many modules support SQLite fallback for their own tables.

Suite-session secret has weak placeholder rejection (`<`, `>`, `replace-`, `change-this` substrings, plus `CHANGE-ME`/`changeme`). A long but low-entropy string passes the 16-char gate; modules relying on this MUST generate from a CSPRNG.
The LLM provider ABC explicitly omits `chat()` and structured tool-use (ADR-0004 §6 defers to v0.3.0 of the LLM surface). Modules needing multi-turn conversation must work around it.

Migration runner intentionally commits independently of the caller's transaction (runner.py docstring): "civiccore commits independently of the caller's transaction. The baseline is idempotent, so a partial-state restart produces the same end-state." Acceptable per ADR-0003 §"Three deployment scenarios" but worth knowing — a failed module migration after civiccore commits leaves the baseline in place.
Reserved-placeholder enforcement is by ADR + reviewer discipline, not by Python — the namespaces are importable (empty `__init__.py`) and downstream modules could shadow them without import errors.

42 pytest tests across 6 test files (tests/test_*.py) covering deterministic helpers, runtime foundation, persistence, auth, and audit:

test_runtime_foundation.py (4 tests): __version__=="0.4.0", pyproject pins published civiccore v1.2.0 wheel, root endpoint states its honest boundary, health returns the civiccore version.

test_accessibility_foundation.py (14 tests): deterministic findings shape (missing body / title / alt-text / long copy / non-English language), plain-language rewrites preserve human-review boundary, language variants flag review_required, accessible export preserves records context, workflow helpers (forms/publishing/ADA/tagged-PDF) cover public-use scope; HTTP-layer tests for /review (token-required success shape), /analyze (stateless, never persists), validation errors (422 with actionable fields/fix), plain-language + language-variant API contracts, public-use workflow routes, adversarial inputs return actionable non-certifying responses, the public UI route renders accessibly and honestly, the staff UI route is API-wired with contract awareness, and the staff page never leaks the write token in HTML.

test_citycore_hardening.py (7 tests): /review write rejects missing-or-wrong token, /records-export write requires the token, 503 when CIVICACCESS_TRUSTED_WRITE_TOKEN is unset, /analyze is open and never persists (probe gap #2 closed), audit_event row persists atomically on review.create, audit_event row persists on records-export (probe gap #3 closed), backup/restore round-trip preserves both review records and audit events (probe gap #4 closed).

test_database_url_selection.py (6 tests): _sync_database_url flips scheme to +psycopg2 for postgres/postgresql, passes through sqlite, preserves credentials that contain scheme-marker substrings; _review_database_url prefers supervisor DATABASE_URL, per-module override wins, falls back to local SQLite when neither is set.

test_postgres_persistence.py (2 tests, gated by CIVICACCESS_POSTGRES_TEST_URL release-gate env): schema creation + round-trip of reviews on real Postgres, review + audit survive engine reconnect (the durability proof, probe gap #4).

test_production_depth_review_persistence.py (9 tests): records persist findings, repository reports schema status, db_admin CLI reports a ready schema, the API persists and retrieves review records, default local DB makes readiness ready, readiness passes with configured schema, lookup reports missing record, lookup uses default DB, /reviews list + /records-export contract.

Net: the suite proves the module is locally durable, atomically audited, write-guarded, schema-versioned, dialect-portable, and HTML-safe. It does NOT prove anything about Tauri wiring, button clicks, or end-to-end browser flows — that lives in the umbrella desktop tests, where civicaccess has effectively no coverage beyond the registry-validation cargo test (which Phase C deleted as redundant).

A clerk who installs the MSI built from civicsuite main 4e0f103 (CI run 28382059243) can do EXACTLY NOTHING related to CivicAccess from the UI. The module is bundled on disk and importable, but every user-reachable surface is missing.

The fallbackState.modules array (desktop/src/main.js:27-153) lists civiccore, civicrecords-ai, civicclerk, civiccode, civicnotice, civiczone — no civicaccess. The navigation array (main.js:17-26) has no "access" entry. MODULE_AREA_BY_ID (main.js:6-11) has no "access" key. CITY_CORE_PRODUCT_MODULE_IDS (main.js:5) is ["civicrecords-ai","civicclerk","civiccode"] — even after Phase C the shipping JS still hardcodes the old 3. EVIDENCE OF ABSENCE — IPC HANDLERS: grep "civicaccess|accessibility-review|records-export|\"access\"" in desktop/src-tauri/src/workflows.rs returns 0 hits. The city_work_action dispatcher (workflows.rs:7667-7783) has no "accessibility-review" => or "records-export" => arm. If anything attempted to invoke them, line 7783 returns Err("Unsupported city workflow action: accessibility-review").

EVIDENCE OF ABSENCE — HTTP SERVICE: services.py runs a stdlib ThreadingHTTPServer on 127.0.0.1:15480 (services.py:18, 184-189) that ONLY answers /health and /modules with the module-import status JSON (services.py:167-178). It does importlib.import_module("civicaccess.main") (services.py:30 OPTIONAL_MODULE_IMPORTS, called by _module_status at services.py:84-102) — that constructs the FastAPI app object in memory but does NOT mount it, does NOT start uvicorn on any port, does NOT proxy /civicaccess/* requests. The civicaccess routes (/civicaccess, /civicaccess/staff, /api/v1/civicaccess/analyze, /api/v1/civicaccess/review, etc.) are unreachable from any client because nothing listens for them. windows-local-runtime.json lists services postgres / python-services / task-queue / model-runtime / file-storage — no civicaccess service entry.

WHAT IS WIRED: (a) services.py:29-31 OPTIONAL_MODULE_IMPORTS has ("civicaccess", "civicaccess.main") so /health on port 15480 reports {id:"civicaccess", ok:true, optional:true, version:"0.4.0"} but a failure there does NOT degrade the overall health (35d6aee inert-fix); (b) migrate.py:72-82 best-effort instantiates AccessibilityReviewRepository(db_url=sync_url) inside try/except so the civicaccess schema gets bootstrapped on Postgres but a failure does not break migration of the shipped 5 (35d6aee inert-fix); (c) supervisor.rs:386-388 generates/reads the secret civicaccess-trusted-write-token.txt and supervisor.rs:2043-2048 injects CIVICACCESS_TRUSTED_WRITE_TOKEN into every Python service child process (so the guard would work IF the service were reachable); (d) auth.rs:539 puts civicaccess in the clerk role's module list alongside civicclerk and civicnotice; (e) main.rs:256 + 262 + 285 declare workflow→module and exports-folder mappings, but no UI emits these actions and no workflows.rs handler exists to receive them; (f) module_registry.rs:1001 cargo-test asserts the default 6-module selection now includes civicaccess.

NET: civicaccess in this MSI is dark code. The schema gets created on first start (best-effort), the write token is provisioned, the module reports healthy in /health JSON, the install plan and verify scripts count 6 modules — but no GUI surface, no clickable button, no reachable HTTP endpoint, no IPC handler exposes any civicaccess capability to the user.

The CSP `connect-src` is `'self' ipc: http://ipc.localhost` (line 28), which technically wouldn't even permit the WebView2 to make XHR/fetch calls to localhost ports like civicaccess's nominal 8060 even if it WERE listening. result.plain_english_summary:
Bottom line: ship the missing UI in one focused pull request that copies what the CivicNotice integration did 5 days ago. Don't roll back the registry change.

Where things stand: the desktop app you install from the latest build (commit 4e0f103) lists six city-core modules in the docs, but the screen still only offers five workflow tabs. A clerk who reads the manual and looks for an Accessibility tab won't find one. The CivicAccess module is technically there — its code is bundled inside the installer, its database tables get created on first run, a secret write-token is provisioned, and the app reports the module as available — but there is no button anywhere in the UI that does anything with it, and no internal network address listens for it. We confirmed this directly: searching the desktop's JavaScript and Rust source for civicaccess returns zero matches in the places that would expose it to a user.

The team did this on purpose in two stages. Phase B (PR #213) wired up everything except the visible UI — the deliberate wired-but-not-yet-offered state. Phase C (PR #214) flipped the documentation to say six modules. Both stages were lockstep registry and plumbing work. The Phase C commit message itself says this is a truth/registry milestone, not the program's done-state.

The recommendation is the smallest path forward that closes the gap and is consistent with how every other module in this app already works: add the JavaScript panel and buttons, add the matching Rust handlers (mirroring exactly what CivicNotice did in PR #193), bump the version to 1.0.2, and ship. The plumbing Phase B installed is the right shape for this. Reverting Phase C is more files changed, more risk, and forces a public we-said-six-now-we-say-five-again reversal across published docs.

If the fix can't ship immediately, add a one-line callout to the manual saying CivicAccess is dark in 1.0.1 and the UI lands in 1.0.2 — that is honest and costs minutes.

options.name: Option A: Forward-fix in ONE lockstep PR (civicnotice pattern, Rust-native)
options.description: Mirror PR #193. Add a renderAccessWorkflow() panel in desktop/src/main.js with data-work-action buttons for accessibility-review, records-export, and any other accessibility actions the staff UI exposes; add fallbackState.modules card for civicaccess; add nav entry 'access'; add MODULE_AREA_BY_ID 'access':'civicaccess'; add CITY_CORE_PRODUCT_MODULE_IDS entry. In desktop/src-tauri/src/workflows.rs, add city_work_action match arms that mutate state.access (a new field on CityWorkState) — either thin wrappers around existing civicaccess Python helpers (PyO3 or subprocess) OR, more consistent with the existing pattern, ports of the deterministic logic from civicaccess/access_review.py, plain_language.py, multilingual.py, workflows.py into Rust. Add one cargo end-to-end test mirroring civicnotice_actions_save_notice_workpaper_and_search_result at workflows.rs:8029. Add one Playwright spec mirroring workflow-pages.spec.mjs:413-460. Bump desktop version 1.0.1 -> 1.0.2 in Cargo.toml + tauri.conf.json. Phase B scaffolding (token, schema, role, folder) needs no changes.
options.cost_estimate: Small-to-medium. The thin-Rust-alias variant (call civicaccess Python helpers via subprocess or PyO3, write results into state.access) is roughly the size of PR #193: ~5-10 Rust handler arms, ~50-100 lines in main.js, ~30 lines of cargo test, ~50 lines of Playwright. Net: 2-5 days for the alias variant, 1-2 weeks for the full port.
risks: Integration risk of new Rust arms + buttons + tests — smaller and more reversible than a registry sweep. Mitigated by the precedent: civicnotice landed in one PR with the same shape.
If subprocess/PyO3 is chosen for the alias variant, introduces a new in-process Python-call pattern Rust doesn't use today (workflows.rs has no PyO3). Full Rust port avoids this entirely.

Full Rust port discards the 42-test Python suite as source of truth for the deterministic helpers — they remain in the civicaccess repo but desktop behavior is now defined by the Rust port. Mitigate with new cargo test + Playwright spec covering the desktop's actual behavior.
Schedule risk if forward-fix slips past Phase D's clean-VM deadline — schedule issue, not correctness issue.

Phase D acceptance becomes 'civicaccess works end-to-end on a clean VM', the natural next milestone after Phase C's truth flip. Reuses every piece of Phase B scaffolding as designed.

options.name: Option B: Spawn civicaccess uvicorn as a 6th supervisor service + iframe the staff page
options.description: Add one service block to desktop/runtime/windows-local-runtime.json mirroring the python-services entry but invoking `runtime/python/python.exe -m uvicorn civicaccess.main:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8060` with HTTP health on /health (default_port 8060 already declared in modules.json:557-637). In desktop/src/main.js add nav chip {id:'access', label:'Accessibility'} and a renderAccessWorkflow() that emits `<iframe src='http://127.0.0.1:8060/civicaccess/staff'>`. No city_work_action arm, no workflows.rs handler. The staff write-token paste flow already exists in civicaccess's own staff page (sessionStorage, never embedded in HTML — main.py:162-167).
options.cost_estimate: Tiny in code (~30 lines: 1 JSON service block + 1 nav entry + 1 iframe panel) but spends architectural budget by introducing a sixth supervisor service and a new desktop pattern (WebView iframing a bundled FastAPI app). No other city-core module does this today.
risks: Introduces a new architecture pattern. Every other city-core module's FastAPI server is bundled-but-unspawned; this would be the first one actually run. Future modules will look at this as precedent and the supervisor grows from 5 services to N.
WebView2 CSP at tauri.conf.json:28 is connect-src 'self' ipc: http://ipc.localhost — must be widened to allow http://127.0.0.1:8060. Small change but a real security surface concern.
The civicaccess staff page is independent UI (its own CSS, its own write-token paste flow) and won't match the look-and-feel of the rest of the desktop. Two distinct UX styles in one app.
Port 8060 must be reserved; not currently used by the supervisor (15432/15480/15434) so fine today but creates a port-allocation responsibility.
Future maintenance: every change to civicaccess HTML/CSS bypasses the desktop's Vite build and accessibility/i18n conventions.

result.recommendation_rationale:
Three reasons, in order of weight.

(1) Phase B did 70% of the work needed for Option A and 0% of the work needed for Option B/C/D specifically. supervisor.rs already provisions and injects CIVICACCESS_TRUSTED_WRITE_TOKEN (supervisor.rs:386-388, 2043-2048); migrate.py already bootstraps the schema (migrate.py:72-82); auth.rs already grants civicaccess to the clerk role (auth.rs:539); main.rs already declares the workflow->module requirement at line 262 ('accessibility-review' | 'records-export' => Some((vec!['civicaccess'], false))), the exports-folder mapping at line 285, and the open-exports-folder routing at line 256; services.py already imports civicaccess for /health (services.py:29-31). The only Phase B asset Option A doesn't immediately consume is the in-memory FastAPI app object — and that's fine, because every other city-core module bundles its FastAPI server unspawned too (civicclerk's 81 routes, civiccode's 50+ routes, civicrecords-ai's 30+ routes, civicnotice's 13 routes — all bundled, none called, business logic reimplemented in Rust against city-work.json). Option A finishes the work Phase B set up for; Options B/C/D throw most of Phase B away.

(2) The civicnotice precedent is a known-good template for exactly this. PR #193 landed civicnotice as ONE lockstep PR ~58 days after the repo was created. The Rust diff was 4 alias arms in workflows.rs:7691-7694, each calling an existing Rust function. The JS diff was 4 data-work-action buttons in a renderNoticeWorkflow() panel at main.js:3422-3434. The test diff was one cargo end-to-end (workflows.rs:8029) + one Playwright spec (workflow-pages.spec.mjs:413-460). CivicAccess is in a better starting position than civicnotice was: Phase B already declared the workflow->module requirement at main.rs:262, so the Rust dispatch arms can land directly without re-declaring role gates.

(3) The alternatives cost more than they save. Option B (uvicorn sidecar + iframe) is smaller in lines but invents a new architecture pattern — every other city-core module is bundled-FastAPI + Rust-native, and adopting B means the next module will face 'should I be like civicnotice or like civicaccess?'. That cost compounds. Option C (revert PR #214) touches ~25 files in lockstep, risks re-introducing the exact launcher/plan drift Blocker 0911dac just fixed, and forces a public six->five->six docs reversal across already-published surfaces — all to mitigate a risk that doesn't exist (user-visible behavior is already identical to the 5-module build because Phase B/C are structurally inert in the UI). The Phase D manifest's rollback_plan is an emergency escape hatch, not the default.

If the forward-fix can't ship before Phase D's clean-VM deadline, Option D (one-line docs callout) is a safe interim — it costs minutes, preserves everything, and is honest. But Option A is the right destination either way.
